nvda: NVIDIA designs the chips behind most AI, but its real lock-in is CUDA, the software millions of engineers already use.
tsla: Tesla sells electric cars and big batteries, but much of its stock-market value rests on its self-driving plans.
ko: Coca-Cola mostly doesn't bottle its own soda. It sells concentrate to independent bottlers, who do the heavy work.
lmt: Lockheed Martin builds fighter jets, missiles and satellites. One jet, the F‑35, is about a quarter of its revenue.
jpm: JPMorgan is two banks in one: Chase branches for households, and a Wall Street arm that brings in slightly more.
cost: Costco caps its markups at about 11⁠–⁠15%. Much of its real profit comes from membership fees, not the goods.
mtd: Mettler-Toledo makes lab and industrial scales, and about a quarter of its sales is servicing the ones it sold.
cboe: Cboe holds the exclusive right to list options on the S&P 500, so no other exchange can compete for that trade.
o: Realty Income owns over 15,000 buildings, and its tenants, not the company, pay the taxes, insurance and upkeep.
fisv: Fiserv is the software behind the scenes: it runs core accounts for banks and card payments for small shops.
pcg: PG&E's model: spend on poles, wires and pipes, then earn a regulator-approved return on that spending.
deck: Deckers owns several shoe brands, but UGG and HOKA alone make up 97.3% of its revenue.
a: Agilent sells lab instruments, but its largest, most profitable unit is the service and supplies that keep them running.
aep: AEP is a regulated utility: profit grows with what it builds, and data-center power contracts give it plenty to build.
amcr: Amcor makes the film, bottles and jars that carry other brands' products — you've used it and never seen its name.
app: AppLovin runs the ad auction, the bidder and the tool that measures if the ad worked — all under one roof.
baba: Alibaba runs China's biggest online marketplaces, but US shareholders own a claim on contracts, not the businesses.
blk: BlackRock runs trillions of other people's money, including iShares funds, and earns fees on it, not on its own bets.
casy: Casey's earns most of its revenue at the pump, but most of its profit from the pizza oven and grocery aisle inside.
chtr: Charter sells home internet under the Spectrum brand and bundles in mobile service to keep customers from switching.
cnp: CenterPoint's Houston utility doesn't sell power — it owns the wires and earns a return on what it builds.
crm: Salesforce charges per user, and its AI agents are built to do people's work, so they could shrink the seats it bills.
dash: DoorDash takes a cut of every order, but ads on its app need no extra courier and earn a far higher margin.
dow: Dow makes basic plastics and chemicals, and its profit swings with their price far more than with how much it sells.
eix: Edison earns a regulated return on the grid it builds, but California law can make it pay for fires its gear starts.
evrg: Evergy earns a regulator-set return on what it builds, and data centers have given a once-flat utility a lot to build.
fe: FirstEnergy's transmission lines earn a return almost the moment they're built, unlike its state-regulated local wires.
ftv: Fortive sells the radiation badges and gas detectors that hospitals and plants dare not switch brands on.
gpc: Genuine Parts sells car parts through NAPA, partly via independently owned stores, and industrial parts through Motion.
hon: Honeywell sells the control systems that run refineries and plants, and earns royalties on plant designs it licenses.
ibm: IBM is mostly cloud software and consulting, but its mainframes still run much of the world's banking and payments.
isrg: Intuitive Surgical earns more from the disposable tools used in each robotic surgery than from selling the robot itself.
kim: Kimco owns grocery-anchored shopping centers; the small shops pay the most rent per foot and leave first in a downturn.
lite: Lumentum makes lasers from indium phosphide, a material that emits light silicon can't, to carry data between AI chips.
mcd: McDonald's earns most of its money as a landlord — rent and royalties from franchisees, not burger sales.
mo: Altria hasn't advertised cigarettes for decades — that ban makes Marlboro's brand impossible for rivals to copy.
mu: Micron makes memory chips, a boom-and-bust trade, but sells some output on multi-year contracts backed by deposits.
nsc: Norfolk Southern is one of only two big freight railroads east of the Mississippi, hauling chemicals, cars and coal.
orcl: Oracle made its name selling the databases big companies run on, and has become a major cloud renting out AI computing.
pgr: Progressive sorts drivers into far finer price groups than rivals, winning good risks and leaving bad ones to others.
psa: Public Storage rents its units month to month, so its prices reset within weeks, both up and down.
rjf: Raymond James sweeps idle client cash into its own bank at a rate it largely sets, then lends it out at a higher one.
sbux: Starbucks runs only about a third of its 40,000-plus stores itself; the other two-thirds are licensed to partners.
sony: Sony earns most of its profit from PlayStation and music, not from the cameras and TVs that made its name.
syf: The store card at Lowe's or the vet's office is often issued by Synchrony — a lender wearing someone else's name.
tm: Toyota reports in yen but sells worldwide, so each one-yen move against the dollar shifts its yearly profit about ¥50B.
tte: TotalEnergies runs oil and gas from well to pump, and is building a power business that earns lower returns than oil.
uri: United Rentals earns twice from every machine: rents it, then sells it used — and that price grades the whole fleet.
vtr: Ventas owns senior housing and mostly keeps the residents' fees and pays running costs, instead of collecting rent.
wrb: W. R. Berkley is a federation of about 60 semi-independent units, each insuring one narrow slice of business risk.
aapl: Apple sells iPhones, but Google pays it an estimated $20–26B a year just to be the default search engine in Safari.
aes: AES builds solar, wind and battery plants and sells the power on long contracts, increasingly to data-center operators.
amd: AMD designs processors for data centers, PCs and game consoles but owns no factories; TSMC makes most of its chips.
aptv: Aptiv makes the connectors, sensors and computers inside cars, and sells the same parts to robots, drones and factories.
bac: Bank of America's edge is cheap money: households' checking accounts fund its loans at a fraction of market rates.
bmy: Bristol Myers Squibb is a drugmaker where one medicine, the blood thinner Eliquis, brings in nearly a third of revenue.
cat: Caterpillar is known for bulldozers, but its biggest unit by sales and profit makes engines and turbines for power.
ci: Cigna looks like a health insurer, but over 80% of its revenue comes from Evernorth, its pharmacy-benefit arm.
cnq: Canadian Natural mines oil sands and upgrades the bitumen into synthetic crude that sells at a premium to regular oil.
crwd: CrowdStrike installs one lightweight sensor, then sells over 30 separately priced security modules off that same data.
dd: DuPont makes specialty materials: Tyvek for medical packaging and protective suits, water filters and device parts.
dpz: Domino's barely sells pizza itself — most revenue is supplying franchised stores and collecting their royalties.
el: Estée Lauder sells prestige beauty, from La Mer to Clinique and M·A·C, and skin care is about half its sales.
ew: Edwards Lifesciences makes heart valves, mostly ones threaded in through an artery instead of by open-chest surgery.
fer: Ferrovial is mostly a builder by revenue, but toll roads, about a sixth of sales, bring in over two-thirds of profit.
gd: General Dynamics is a defense contractor, but its most profitable business builds civilian Gulfstream jets, not weapons.
gpn: Global Payments does one job: it helps over 6 million merchant locations in 175-plus countries accept card payments.
hona: Honeywell Aerospace makes airplane parts, but about 45% of sales come from planes already flying, not new jets.
ice: ICE owns the New York Stock Exchange, but its edge is owning the Brent oil price other contracts are written against.
it: Gartner sells research subscriptions, and a vendor's ranking in its reports can make or break its sales.
kkr: KKR owns a life insurer, Global Atlantic, because policyholders' long-term money is capital it can invest for fees.
lly: Eli Lilly's two biggest drugs, Mounjaro and Zepbound, are the same molecule sold under different names.
mchp: Microchip makes the small control chips in factory gear and cars, and sells data centers the plumbing around AI chips.
mos: Mosaic is a spread business: it buys sulfur and ammonia, reacts them with mined phosphate rock and sells the fertilizer.
mufg: MUFG is Japan's largest bank group, and much of its overseas profit comes from the quarter of Morgan Stanley it owns.
ntap: NetApp sells storage hardware, but Microsoft, Amazon and Google also sell its cloud storage as their own service.
orly: O'Reilly Auto Parts wins repair shops on speed, not price: an idle repair bay costs a mechanic more than a pricier part.
ph: Parker Hannifin is known for hydraulics, but aircraft parts are a third of its sales and an even bigger share of profit.
psky: Paramount Skydance owns CBS, cable channels like Nickelodeon and MTV, and Paramount+, earning ads and carriage fees.
rklb: Rocket Lab builds and launches rockets, but most of its revenue comes from building satellites, not launching them.
schw: Charles Schwab looks like a discount broker, but it earns more from clients' idle cash than from their trades.
spcx: SpaceX is famous for rockets, but Starlink internet brings in over half its revenue; launch is its smallest business.
syk: Stryker's Mako robot does over two-thirds of its U.S. knee replacements, and each one locks surgeons into its implants.
tmo: Thermo Fisher sells lab and drug-making supplies; once one is in a drug's regulatory filing, swapping it is costly.
ttwo: Take-Two sells games, but most of its money comes after the sale, from in-game currency, add-ons and subscriptions.
usb: U.S. Bancorp earns over 40% of revenue from fees, far above most regional banks, thanks to a big card and payments arm.
vtrs: Viatris sells old, off-patent brand-name drugs — in China those names still sell at a premium over generics.
wsm: Williams-Sonoma sells its own designs, like Pottery Barn, so no one can list the same sofa cheaper: it holds full price.
abbv: Half of AbbVie's sales are immune-disease drugs, and it sells more Botox for medical uses like migraine than for looks.
afl: Aflac pays cash for cancer and accident claims — but Japan, not the US, supplies two-thirds of its profit.
ame: AMETEK buys small makers of niche instruments, then lifts their margins from the high teens toward its own high 20s.
are: Alexandria is landlord to the lab bench: it rents wet-lab campuses to life-science firms beside top universities.
ball: Ball makes almost nothing but aluminium cans, passing metal costs to customers so revenue can rise without extra profit.
bn: Brookfield earns fees managing others' money, and invests its insurers' policyholder cash partly in its own funds.
cb: Chubb earns twice: it prices insurance more profitably than most rivals, then invests the premiums it holds meanwhile.
cien: Ciena makes the fiber-optic gear linking data centers, and sells its own optical chips in systems and plug-in modules.
cof: Capital One is mainly a card lender, and apart from Amex it's the only US card issuer that owns its own payment network.
crwv: CoreWeave rents Nvidia's chips to AI companies. Nvidia is also its supplier, a shareholder, and its backstop buyer.
ddog: Datadog charges by usage, not by seat — revenue rises as a customer's servers grow, and falls when they don't.
dri: Darden runs Olive Garden and other chains, buying regional brands and plugging them into one shared purchasing machine.
elv: Elevance sells Blue Cross Blue Shield plans in 14 states, with its own drug-benefit middleman keeping pharmacy profit.
exc: Exelon owns the wires, not the power plants, so it earns a regulator-set return on its grid, not on the price of power.
ferg: Ferguson makes little of what it sells: it gets pipes, valves and heating gear to job sites fast, on credit.
gddy: GoDaddy sells domain names as the hook, then tries to sell everything that hangs off one — hosting, a website, email.
grmn: Garmin sells GPS watches and boat gear, but its fattest margins come from certified cockpit electronics, slow to copy.
hood: Robinhood's free trades are paid for by the firms that fill them, who pay far more for options orders than for stocks.
idxx: IDEXX sells vets blood-testing machines at modest margins, then sells test supplies that only run on those machines.
itw: ITW runs about 80 small industrial units on one rule: back the 20% of customers and products that make 80% of sales.
klac: KLA doesn't make chips — it makes machines that catch defects in chips as they're made, with about 56% of that market.
lnt: Alliant is a monopoly utility in Iowa and Wisconsin; regulators let it earn a set return on what it invests in the grid.
mck: McKesson delivers drugs to nearly every US pharmacy and hospital, keeping under 2 cents of profit per dollar of sales.
mpc: Marathon isn't betting on oil prices — it buys crude and sells fuel, earning the gap, which can widen even as oil falls.
nbis: Nebius rents Nvidia chip power to AI labs from servers it designs itself; big customers often prepay much of the build.
ntrs: Northern Trust charges fees to safekeep other people's investments and, unlike its two big rivals, runs a private bank.
otis: Otis earns about 3 cents per dollar selling new elevators, but over 20 cents servicing them for decades afterwards.
phm: Pulte builds under three brands: Centex for first-time buyers, Pulte for move-up families and Del Webb for over-55s.
psx: Phillips 66 refines oil, but its steadier profit is fees from the pipelines and gas plants it runs, not refining.
rl: Ralph Lauren sells the logo: discounting less, it keeps about 70 cents of each sales dollar after the cost of the goods.
se: Sea Limited runs e-commerce, lending and gaming under one roof — gaming, just 10% of revenue, earns the most profit.
spg: Simon owns top US malls and outlets; since almost no new malls get built, retailers wanting those spots pay up for them.
syy: Sysco delivers food to about 700,000 kitchens and keeps just 2 cents of every dollar — thin margins, huge volume.
tmus: T-Mobile sells phone plans, and resells its network's idle capacity as home internet at almost no extra cost to run.
txn: Texas Instruments makes simple power and signal chips for cars and factories in its own plants; many rivals outsource.
v: Visa never lends anyone money. It just charges a small fee on every card swipe and takes none of the credit risk.
vz: Verizon earns most of its money on monthly wireless plans, and bundles home internet so customers stay longer.
wst: West doesn't make drugs. It makes the rubber stoppers that touch them inside the vial, rarely swapped once approved.
abnb: Airbnb owns no property. It charges fees to both guests and hosts, keeping roughly 13 cents of every booking dollar.
aig: AIG sells property and liability insurance worldwide, mostly to businesses, and invests premiums until claims come due.
amgn: Amgen, the original biotech, sells about two dozen medicines, and none brings in more than about 11% of revenue.
ares: Ares earns fees managing other people's money, about two-thirds of it lent out, much of it directly to mid-sized firms.
bax: Baxter makes hospital basics like IV fluids and infusion pumps; each pump placed keeps selling its sets and fluids.
bns: Scotiabank is a Canadian bank with a second home in Latin America, where lending pays more but carries more risk.
cbre: CBRE leases, sells and runs commercial property; about 40% of revenue is client payroll passed on at near-zero profit.
cinf: Cincinnati Financial insures firms, homes and cars, with about 40% of its investments in stocks that swing its profit.
cohr: Coherent makes optical modules that link AI chips — and, unusually, grows its own laser chips instead of buying them.
csco: Cisco sells the switches and routers behind the internet, then earns steady support fees on the gear already installed.
de: Deere builds tractors and combines, and runs its own bank that lends farmers and dealers the money to buy them.
dte: DTE, Detroit's power company, earns a state-set return on the poles, wires and plants regulators let it build.
eme: EMCOR installs the wiring, piping and cooling inside data centers and hospitals, and services those systems afterwards.
exe: Expand Energy is America's largest gas producer; the same gas earns very different prices by pipeline access.
ffiv: F5 sits in front of companies' apps, routing traffic and blocking attacks; support contracts are about half its sales.
ge: GE Aerospace sells jet engines at thin or even negative margins, then profits for 25 to 30 years on parts and servicing.
gs: Goldman Sachs earns about two-thirds of its revenue advising on deals and trading, and most of the rest managing money.
hpe: HPE sells companies servers, storage and networking gear, and runs a leasing arm that finances the purchases.
iex: IDEX makes small parts like pumps, valves and filters that cost little next to the machine but are risky to swap out.
ivz: Invesco manages money for a fee; its giant Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ has only paid it a management fee since late 2025.
kmb: Kimberly-Clark makes throwaway staples like Huggies and Kleenex, sold mostly via giant retailers who control the shelf.
low: Lowe's sells mostly to do-it-yourself homeowners from over 1,700 stores, and owns distributors that supply contractors.
mco: Moody's is two businesses under one name: a toll booth on new debt sales, and a separate subscription data business.
mpwr: Monolithic Power owns a proprietary chip-making process but rents the factories — differentiated silicon, no fab to own.
nclh: Norwegian runs three cruise lines; about a third of its revenue is what passengers spend on board, on top of the ticket.
nu: Nubank has no branches — it spends about $1 a month to serve a customer and earns about $17 from one.
oxy: Occidental pumps oil and gas, mostly in the Permian Basin, and is developing machines that pull CO2 from the air.
pkg: Packaging Corp makes the cardboard in its own mills and mostly sells it to itself — its own box plants.
ptc: PTC sells the software that holds a product's design history — switching means redoing years of regulatory paperwork.
rmd: ResMed sells sleep apnea machines, then keeps selling the masks and tubing patients replace on a schedule for years.
shel: Shell doesn't just sell oil and gas — it trades cargoes globally, moving them to wherever the price is highest.
spgi: S&P Global rates debt and owns the S&P 500, taking a small yearly cut of the money in funds that license its indexes.
t: AT&T sells wireless and fiber home internet, and households that buy both are much less likely to cancel either.
tpl: Texas Pacific Land was formed in 1888 to sell a failed railroad's land; it never finished, and collects oil royalties.
txt: Textron builds Cessna and Beechcraft planes and Bell helicopters, then earns for decades servicing the fleet in the air.
veev: Veeva sells the software that health regulators audit — switching isn't an IT project, it's a compliance event.
wab: Wabtec's locomotives run for 30-40 years, and it almost always services and overhauls them itself — no real competition.
wtw: WTW insures nothing: it earns fees finding insurance for companies and advising employers on pensions, benefits and pay.
abt: Abbott sells diabetes sensors, lab tests and baby formula; users swap a sensor every 14 days, so each one keeps paying.
aiz: Assurant is the insurer behind other brands: phone cover sold by carriers, home cover lenders buy when yours lapses.
amp: Ameriprise pays its financial advisors once, then earns three times: an advice fee, a product fee and cash interest.
arm: Arm earns a royalty on every Arm-based chip that ships, and also sells its own chips against the customers paying it.
bby: Best Buy is the last nationwide gadget showroom, but sells the same products as online stores, so margins stay near 4%.
bny: BNY is more custodian than bank: it safeguards over $60 trillion of others' assets, and about 70% of revenue is fees.
ccep: CCEP bottles Coca-Cola under licence; the Coca-Cola Company owns 18% of it and takes a cut of every price rise it makes.
cl: Colgate holds over 40% of the global toothpaste market, but its Hill's pet food brings in over a fifth of sales.
coin: Coinbase is more than a crypto exchange: a fifth to a quarter of revenue is interest on USDC, a digital dollar.
csgp: CoStar's profit comes from a commercial-property database brokers rely on; its home sites bring growth, not profit.
dell: Most of the cost inside a Dell AI server is a bought-in GPU chip, so it earns far less margin than a normal server.
duk: Duke Energy earns a regulator-approved return on what it spends building the grid, not on selling power.
emr: Emerson makes industrial valves and sensors; adding AspenTech software helped lift gross margin from 44% (2021) to 53%.
expd: Expeditors owns no ships or planes; it buys cargo space and resells it. Customs paperwork is its biggest profit pool.
fico: FICO doesn't collect your credit data - the bureaus do. It licenses the algorithm that turns it into your score.
gehc: GE HealthCare's contrast dyes and tracers are 14% of sales but over a quarter of profit: twice its scanners' margin.
gww: Grainger sells industrial supplies two ways: sales reps and branches, or Zoro, an online marketplace growing faster.
hpq: HP sells PCs and printers: PCs bring in three-quarters of revenue, but printing earns nearly four times their margin.
iff: You've never bought anything from IFF, but you've used its products - it designs the smell and taste in others' brands.
j: Jacobs designs water systems, power grids and chip plants; over a quarter of revenue is pass-through cost, not margin.
kmi: Kinder Morgan earns long-term fees for piping natural gas, but nearly a tenth of its profit comes from producing oil.
lrcx: Lam Research makes chip-etching machines, but over a third of revenue is parts and service for ones already installed.
mdlz: Mondelez sells Oreo, Ritz and Cadbury in about 150 countries, and Europe, not the US, is its biggest market by sales.
mrk: One drug, Keytruda, is roughly half of Merck's revenue - and it loses US patent protection in 2028.
ndaq: Nasdaq is mostly not a stock exchange: over three-quarters of revenue is index licensing, data and software for banks.
nue: Nucor melts scrap metal into steel rather than smelting iron ore, so it can idle furnaces instead of losing money.
p: Everpure, ex-Pure Storage, sells all-flash storage that runs raw flash chips with its own software, not stock drives.
pld: Prologis is the world's largest warehouse owner; much of its growth comes as old leases signed below market rent reset.
pwr: Quanta builds the power grid, and its growth is capped by how fast it can train linemen - so it owns a lineman college.
rok: Rockwell sells factory controllers; its moat is that most North American plant engineers learned on Allen-Bradley kit.
shop: Shopify keeps about 3 cents of every dollar its merchants sell, mostly from payments, not its monthly plan fees.
spot: Spotify doesn't own the music it streams - four label groups supply about 72% of it and can reprice it at renewal.
td: TD is a Canadian bank that also runs over 1,000 US branches from Maine to Florida; Canadian banking is its biggest arm.
tpr: Tapestry renamed itself from Coach to sound like a house of brands, but Coach alone still brings in over 80% of sales.
tyl: Tyler runs the software behind courthouses and tax offices, and takes a fee when citizens pay fines or bills online.
vici: VICI owns the land and buildings under over 100 casinos and resorts, and rents them out on leases lasting decades.
wat: Waters sells lab machines that tell drug makers what is in a sample; about half its sales are refills and service after.
wy: Weyerhaeuser's trees are a bet on housing that pays you to wait - if lumber is cheap, it just leaves them standing.
acgl: Arch Capital writes insurance and reinsurance. Its smallest line, mortgage cover, earns a third of underwriting profit.
ajg: Arthur J. Gallagher is an insurance broker, not an insurer — it earns commission on policies and never pays a claim.
amt: American Tower rents space on cell towers to phone carriers — adding a second tenant costs it almost nothing more.
asml: ASML is the only company on earth that makes EUV chipmaking machines — and the only one that can service them too.
bdx: Becton Dickinson makes hospital basics like syringes and IV lines, plus prefillable syringes that deliver GLP-1 drugs.
br: Broadridge processes proxy votes for almost every US public company, and gets paid per brokerage account, not per sale.
cci: Crown Castle owns about 40,000 cell towers and rents space to phone carriers. Three carriers pay 93% of the rent.
cls: Celestica builds network switches and servers for AI data centers — badged with customers' brands, not its own.
coo: Cooper Companies is two businesses in one ticker: CooperVision's contact lenses, CooperSurgical's fertility supplies.
csx: CSX is one of only two major railroads east of the Mississippi. Nobody is laying 20,000 more miles of track to compete.
dg: Dollar General runs over 21,000 small stores, usually in towns with room for one discount store but not two.
dva: DaVita runs dialysis clinics. Government programs cover 89% of patients; commercial insurers supply nearly all profit.
enb: Enbridge moves oil through pipelines nobody could permit today — its main line is so full that shippers get rationed.
expe: Expedia sells trips under its own brands, and earns about a third of revenue running bookings for airlines and banks.
fis: FIS is plumbing for banks: it runs the core account systems, card issuing and payment processing much of banking uses.
gen: Gen Digital sells antivirus under Norton and Avast — and, since buying MoneyLion, also makes short-term consumer loans.
hal: Halliburton doesn't own a drop of oil. It rents out the crews, equipment and know-how that get it out of the ground.
hrl: Hormel owns SPAM, Skippy and Planters, but its best margins come from selling meat to restaurants, not grocery shelves.
ilmn: Illumina's sequencing machines are the razor. The reagents a lab must keep buying are the blade — two-thirds of revenue.
jbht: J.B. Hunt's biggest business isn't trucking — it owns the containers and rents the long middle from the railroads.
kr: Kroger sells groceries at roughly 2% margin — selling ad space to food brands off shopper data is far more profitable.
lulu: Lululemon sells its own clothes through its own stores, keeping the retail markup most apparel brands hand away.
mdt: Medtronic is the largest pure medical-device maker, and it makes more than half of all pacemakers implanted worldwide.
mrna: Moderna's medicines are instructions, not drugs — mRNA that tells a patient's own cells to make a target protein.
ndsn: Nordson makes machines that dispense a precise dot of glue or coating — and earns technology-company margins doing it.
nvo: Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy are one molecule, semaglutide, under two names. Together they are two-thirds of sales.
panw: Palo Alto Networks is the largest pure cybersecurity firm, grown from firewalls into cloud security and identity.
pltr: Palantir doesn't train AI models. It builds the data layer that lets any model act on a customer's real operations.
pypl: PayPal earns a fat fee when shoppers click its button, and a thin one quietly running card payments for big merchants.
rol: Rollins, parent of Orkin, sends technicians to the same homes every month or quarter. Dense routes are the moat.
shw: Sherwin-Williams owns the stores it sells paint from, so it keeps the retail markup Behr hands over to Home Depot.
sre: Sempra owns a stake in Oncor, Texas's largest power-line utility, so it books a share of Oncor's profit but no revenue.
tdg: TransDigm makes aircraft parts so specialized that switching suppliers means recertifying the plane.
trgp: Targa gathers and processes Permian gas, then moves and exports its liquids. One molecule can pay Targa four times.
ual: United Airlines flies out of hubs like Newark and O'Hare — you cannot build a second Newark.
vlo: Valero refines crude into fuel and profits on the 'crack spread' — the gap between crude cost and fuel price.
wbd: Warner Bros. Discovery owns HBO, CNN and the Warner studio, but its shrinking cable channels still earn the most profit.
wynn: Wynn Resorts runs casinos in Las Vegas, Macau and Boston. Its profits swing on how lucky the tables ran that quarter.
acn: Accenture sells its people's time: revenue is headcount times hours billed times rate, so saving hours cuts revenue.
akam: Akamai is known for speeding websites and video around the world, yet security is its biggest business.
amzn: Amazon's online store runs on thin margins. Its cloud arm, AWS, earns more than half of the company's operating profit.
ato: Atmos doesn't sell gas for profit — it earns a regulator-set return on the pipes it builds.
be: Bloom's fuel cells aren't the cheapest power. They sell on speed: running on site in months, not years of grid waits.
brkb: Berkshire's real business is insurance: it holds $177B of premiums before claims, investing that money almost free.
ccl: Carnival sells cruise tickets, but about a third of its revenue comes from what passengers spend once they are on board.
clx: Clorox is more than bleach: it also sells Glad bags, Kingsford charcoal, Hidden Valley dressing and Burt's Bees.
cop: ConocoPhillips only finds and sells oil and gas. With no refineries or chemical plants, its profit tracks fuel prices.
ctas: Cintas rents uniforms, but the same truck also sells first-aid restocking and fire-extinguisher checks.
dgx: Quest's product is a blood test, but its real business is logistics: moving tubes from doctors' offices to labs.
dvn: Devon counts oil and gas in one unit, barrels of oil equivalent, but a gas barrel earns a small fraction of an oil one.
eog: EOG sells much of its own oil via Gulf Coast and export outlets rather than at the well, fetching above US benchmarks.
exr: Extra Space doesn't just rent storage units — it also sells insurance on what's inside them, keeping premiums itself.
fitb: Fifth Third is a regional bank, and over a quarter of its deposits pay no interest: free money it lends out at a profit.
gev: GE Vernova builds turbines and grid gear. Plants using its machines make a quarter of the world's electricity.
has: Hasbro is known for toys, but its biggest earner is Wizards of the Coast, home of Magic: The Gathering and D&D.
hsbc: HSBC is based in London, but its Asian bank, centred on Hong Kong, earns about two-thirds of the group's profit.
incy: Incyte's whole business rests on one drug, Jakafi, worth 60% of revenue — and its patent protection runs out in 2028.
jbl: Jabil builds servers, medical devices and gadgets under other brands — but keeps only nine cents per dollar of sales.
kvue: Kenvue is J&J's former consumer arm: Tylenol, Band-Aid, Listerine and Neutrogena, all sold without a prescription.
luv: Southwest built its brand on free bags and open seating, then dropped both to earn money from bag fees and paid seats.
meli: MercadoLibre is called the Amazon of Latin America, but it is also a lender, with a credit book of over $16B.
mrsh: Marsh & McLennan insures nothing. As a broker it earns a cut of each premium, so revenue moves with insurance prices.
nee: NextEra is two firms: Florida Power & Light, a regulated utility, and North America's largest wind and solar developer.
nvr: NVR builds homes but mostly avoids owning land: it controls lots through options and deposits, buying them as it builds.
payx: Paychex runs payroll for about 800,000 small and mid-sized employers, and earns interest on the payroll cash it holds.
pm: Philip Morris International sells Marlboro in about 175 markets, but not the US, where cigarettes stayed with Altria.
q: Qnity makes the chemicals and materials every chip has to pass through to exist — and almost nobody has heard of it.
rop: Roper buys and holds niche software firms, from legal practice tools to utility billing, that customers rarely leave.
sjm: Smucker sells coffee, peanut butter, pet food and Twinkies; coffee is over a third of sales, pet food the best margin.
ste: STERIS sterilizes for device makers whose methods are written into regulatory filings, so switching means re-validating.
tdy: Teledyne makes sensors for places people can't easily go; imaging, from thermal cameras to satellites, is over half.
tri: Thomson Reuters sells research tools lawyers and accountants can't get wrong, built on its own editorial notes on law.
uber: Uber owns essentially none of the cars on its app. It keeps a cut of every fare, so it spends little on equipment.
vlto: Veralto, once part of Danaher, has two quiet trades: testing and treating water, and printing date codes on food packs.
wday: Workday rents out HR and finance software and charges by the seat, so AI that does staff's work is its biggest risk.
xel: Xcel doesn't sell electricity for profit — it earns a regulator-approved return on what it builds.
adbe: Adobe rents Photoshop and Acrobat by subscription, and it invented PDF, the most durable piece of the whole business.
alab: Astera makes no AI processors; it sells the chips that keep GPUs, memory and network cards talking at full speed.
anet: Arista sells network switches, but its real edge is running one identical software image on every one of them.
avgo: Broadcom co-designs custom AI chips for tech giants; its VMware software arm supplies steady cash between chip cycles.
ben: Franklin Templeton is an asset manager, earning a fee on every dollar of the over $1.7 trillion it manages for others.
bro: Brown & Brown sells insurance but never pays a claim — it just earns a commission and leaves the risk to the insurer.
cdns: Cadence sells the software chip designers use, plus special machines that run a chip's design before any silicon exists.
cmcsa: Comcast is mostly cable internet. Its mobile plans run on Verizon's network, sold cheaply in a bundle so homes stay.
cor: Cencora, one of three firms moving nearly all US prescriptions, keeps under 1% of sales; generics carry its margin.
ctsh: Cognizant's product is its people's time: some 350,000 staff whose billable hours are what clients pay for.
dhi: D.R. Horton, the biggest US homebuilder, aims at entry-level buyers and runs its own mortgage lender to close sales.
dxcm: DexCom doesn't really sell a device — it sells a sensor that wears out every 10 to 15 days, so patients reorder.
eqix: Equinix rents data-center space, then charges again for cables linking one tenant to another, at almost no extra cost.
f: Ford's fleet arm, selling vans and trucks to businesses, earns about half its segment profit on a third of its sales.
fix: Comfort Systems installs wiring, cooling and piping in buildings, often as modules built first in its own factories.
gild: Gilead is mostly an HIV business: its HIV drugs are about 70% of sales, and a single pill, Biktarvy, is nearly half.
hban: Huntington funds fast-growing Texas and Southeast loans with cheap deposits gathered back home in the Midwest.
hsic: Henry Schein sells dental supplies on thin margins, but its practice software keeps dentists loyal to reorder from it.
intc: Intel designs and builds its own chips, rare among big chipmakers, and its factory arm mostly makes chips for Intel.
jci: Johnson Controls installs cooling and fire systems in big buildings, then earns about 30% of its sales servicing them.
l: Loews isn't an insurer — it's a family holding company that also owns a gas pipeline network and a hotel chain.
lvs: Las Vegas Sands runs no casinos in Las Vegas — most of its profit comes from one building in Singapore.
met: MetLife sells life and benefits cover, largely via employers, and invests the premiums for decades before paying claims.
mrvl: Marvell co-designs custom AI chips for cloud giants like Amazon and Microsoft, plus optical chips linking AI racks.
nem: Newmont, the world's largest gold miner, has mostly fixed costs, so swings in the gold price hit its profit hard.
nvs: Novartis shed its generics and eye-care arms, so it sells only patented drugs and must keep replacing those that expire.
pcar: PACCAR sells trucks at thin margins, but replacement parts are under a quarter of revenue and about half its profit.
pnc: PNC lends mostly to businesses, and nearly a quarter of its deposits pay no interest, which makes its funding cheap.
qcom: Qualcomm sells phone chips, and also collects a royalty on nearly every phone made, even those with no Qualcomm chip.
rost: Ross Stores buys brands' excess stock for cash, with no returns, and sells it 20 to 60% below department-store prices.
slb: SLB is the contractor oil companies hire to find, drill and run wells, and nearly 80% of its revenue comes from abroad.
stld: Steel Dynamics doesn't mine iron ore — it melts scrap metal and profits on the gap between scrap and steel prices.
tech: Bio-Techne sells lab reagents that scientists build experiments around — switching means re-validating the work.
trmb: Trimble began in GPS survey gear and added design and building software, made so each tool shares data with the next.
udr: UDR rents out about 60,000 apartments; most profit comes from coastal cities, where new building is slow and costly.
vmc: Vulcan sells crushed rock, so heavy and cheap that trucking it far costs more than the rock is worth.
wdc: Western Digital and Seagate make about 95% of the world's hard-drive capacity, and cloud data centers buy most of it.
xom: At Exxon, refining brings in most of the revenue, but drilling for oil and gas brings in most of the profit.
adm: ADM turns crops into oil, starch and ethanol; its wafer-thin 2% profit margin is normal, not a warning sign.
algn: Align sells Invisalign aligners but prices its iTero scanners cheap to turn more scans into aligner sales.
aos: A. O. Smith sells water heaters nobody thinks about until one bursts; about 80 to 85% of US home demand is replacement.
awk: American Water owns the pipes — no one competes for your hookup. It earns a state-approved return on what it builds.
bg: Bunge crushes crops into animal feed and cooking oil, but keeps only about a penny of profit per dollar of sales.
bx: Blackstone manages over $1 trillion, and nearly half its fee-paying money is permanent, so it never has to be re-raised.
ceg: Constellation runs the largest US nuclear fleet, and a federal tax credit sets a price floor under that nuclear power.
cmg: Unlike most big chains, Chipotle owns its US restaurants rather than franchising, so it keeps all the margin and cost.
cpay: Corpay began with fuel cards for truckers and takes a small cut of business spending, from fuel to payments abroad.
cvna: Carvana sells used cars online, and usually writes the buyer's loan too, then sells that loan on for a second profit.
dis: Disney's parks, cruises and merchandise arm is its biggest profit engine, at about double the margin of the rest.
echo: EchoStar's main asset was airwaves bought over 20 years, worth far more than its shrinking TV, phone and satellite arms.
erie: Erie Indemnity isn't the insurer: it manages Erie Insurance Exchange for up to 25% of premiums, with no claims risk.
fast: Fastenal sells nuts, bolts and gloves; nearly half its sales go through vending machines and bins in customers' plants.
flut: Flutter, FanDuel's owner, needn't know who wins: it prices both sides of a bet to keep a steady slice of every dollar.
gl: Globe Life sells life and health cover to lower- and middle-income families, through agents it recruits and runs itself.
hd: Home Depot looks like a DIY store, but pros, who make about one in ten purchases, bring in roughly half its sales.
hsy: Hershey is mostly North American candy, nearly four-fifths of sales, so the price of cocoa largely sets its profit.
invh: Invitation Homes rents out over 100,000 houses; its biggest cost, property tax, is set by county assessors.
jnj: J&J is the only company in the top three in both drugs and medical devices, with over two dozen $1 billion lines.
len: Lennar builds homes but owns almost no land: of the lots it controls, it owns about 2% and buys the rest just in time.
lyv: Concerts bring Live Nation over 80% of revenue but only a quarter of profit; ticketing and sponsorship earn the rest.
mgm: MGM runs Las Vegas casino resorts but sold much of the real estate, so it pays rent on buildings it operates.
msci: MSCI licenses stock indexes to funds, often for a cut of their assets; switching means renaming the fund, so few leave.
ni: NiSource, mostly a gas utility, serves Amazon and Google via a separate power company so ordinary customers don't pay.
nxpi: NXP sells chips for car brakes and airbags, not AI data centers — it earns more as each car model carries more silicon.
peg: PSEG is mostly a New Jersey wires-and-pipes utility, plus nuclear plants whose revenue has a federal tax-credit floor.
pnw: Pinnacle West owns Arizona's biggest utility, which earns a state-set return on what it builds and runs a nuclear plant.
rcl: Royal Caribbean prices cabins for two, so every extra third or fourth guest brings some of its most profitable revenue.
rtx: RTX's Pratt & Whitney sells jet engines at or below cost — the real profit comes later, from spare parts and repairs.
sna: Snap-on sells tools from vans visiting mechanics weekly, often on credit; its lending arm earns about a fifth of profit.
stx: Seagate is one of three firms still making hard drives, and cloud data centers storing AI data are about 80% of sales.
ter: Teradyne makes no chips. With one Japanese rival, it builds nearly all the machines that test chips before they ship.
trv: Travelers earns twice: when premiums exceed claims, and by investing the premiums until those claims are paid.
ul: Unilever sells soap, shampoo, deodorant and detergent worldwide, and grows mainly in emerging markets like India.
vrsk: Verisk pools claims data insurers hand over, then sells the aggregated picture back to those same insurers.
well: Welltower doesn't just collect rent on senior housing — it runs the buildings and keeps the full profit, and the loss.
xyz: Block runs Square and Cash App. Bitcoin sales are roughly a third of its revenue yet only a sliver of its gross profit.
adp: ADP runs payroll for millions of workers, and earns real profit on interest from the cash it holds before paying it out.
all: Allstate sells car and home insurance, yet over 80% of its policies are warranties and protection plans, not insurance.
apa: APA pumps oil and gas in Texas and Egypt. In Egypt the hard part is not finding oil but getting paid by the state buyer.
axon: Axon sells Tasers and body cameras to police, then the cloud software that stores the evidence, at higher margins.
bhp: BHP is known for iron ore, but it is the world's largest copper producer, and copper brings in over half its profit.
bxp: BXP owns trophy office towers in six US cities and signs leases lasting close to a decade, locking in rent for years.
cf: CF Industries turns cheap natural gas into fertilizer, so its profit is the gap between gas cost and fertilizer price.
cmi: Cummins is known for truck engines, but its power-generation arm, big in data-center backup, earns a third of profit.
cprt: Copart auctions wrecked cars for insurers, usually without owning them: it earns fees from both seller and buyer.
cvs: CVS is an insurer, drug-benefit manager and pharmacy chain in one, but earns about a penny of profit per revenue dollar.
dlr: Digital Realty rents data-center space to cloud giants, but its edge is grid power it has secured that rivals can't buy.
ecl: Ecolab sells cleaning chemicals, but the chemistry is only half of what customers pay for — the rest is service.
es: Eversource delivers power and gas across New England and earns a regulator-set return on the wires and pipes it builds.
fcx: Freeport mines copper, but gold and silver credits at its Indonesian mine make copper cost less than nothing there.
foxa: Fox Corporation is the live news and sports Disney didn't buy, paid for by pay-TV fees and advertising.
glw: Corning makes the cover glass on iPhones, but its fastest-growing line is fiber-optic cable linking AI data centers.
hdb: HDFC Bank is India's largest private bank, a deposit-funded lender that also absorbed its former parent's mortgage book.
hubb: Hubbell makes the hardware between the power station and your wall socket — parts nobody ever photographs.
ip: International Paper makes containerboard in its own mills, then turns it into the brown corrugated boxes goods ship in.
kdp: Keurig Dr Pepper sells Keurig brewers near cost and earns on the pods, alongside sodas like Dr Pepper and Canada Dry.
lh: Labcorp runs blood tests nationwide, and grows partly by buying hospitals' outreach labs and folding them in.
ma: Mastercard runs the network, not the cards: banks issue them, and it takes a fee per payment at almost no extra cost.
mkc: McCormick sells spices under its own name, and about 40% of its sales are flavors it supplies to other food makers.
msft: Microsoft earns about as much renting Azure cloud computing as from Office, Teams and LinkedIn, each ~42% of sales.
nke: Nike sells its shoes and sportswear two ways: through retailers like Foot Locker, and through its own stores and app.
odfl: Old Dominion fills shared trailers with freight from shippers too small to fill one, and keeps spare room in downturns.
pep: PepsiCo owns its North American bottling plants, unlike Coca-Cola — and its lower profit margins show it.
podd: Insulet's insulin pump is disposable, worn for a few days then thrown away — so patients rebuy one constantly.
rddt: Reddit's biggest traffic source, Google, is also a paying customer for its data and the AI that competes for readers.
rvty: Revvity is the part of PerkinElmer that stayed public: lab instruments and tests, half for research, half diagnostics.
sndk: SanDisk makes memory chips, but shares its factories 50/50 with Kioxia — a partner and a direct rival at once.
stz: Constellation Brands holds the US rights to Corona and Modelo, brewed in Mexico, and beer is over 90% of its sales.
tfc: Truist, formed from BB&T and SunTrust, is a plain spread lender: it earns the gap between loan rates and deposit costs.
tsco: Tractor Supply's biggest category is feed and supplies for livestock and horses, bought every week, unlike its tools.
ulta: Ulta sells drugstore and department-store beauty brands in the same aisle, with a salon chair at the back.
vrsn: VeriSign is the only operator of the .com registry, and may raise its price by up to 7% in four of every six years.
wfc: Wells Fargo is still mostly a lender: loans to households and mid-sized firms bring in about 58% of its revenue.
yum: KFC, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut are mostly franchised, so Yum keeps only about 13 cents of each dollar their stores take.
adsk: Autodesk sells design software, but architects rarely switch — its drawing file format is the real lock-in.
alle: Allegion makes commercial door locks. Architects specify the brand once; buildings replace it for decades.
apd: Air Products builds gas plants inside customers' factories, then charges a minimum fee whether they use the gas or not.
axp: Amex is the card, the network and the lender at once: it earns merchant fees, annual card fees and interest on balances.
biib: Biogen sells brain and nerve drugs, and nearly a fifth of its revenue is royalties on drugs Roche sells, like Ocrevus.
c: Citigroup moves about $5 trillion a day for multinationals in roughly 90 countries: the plumbing of global trade.
cfg: Citizens is a regional bank with about 1,000 branches in 14 states, lending out deposits at a higher rate than it pays.
cms: CMS Energy earns mainly by building Michigan power lines and pipes, on which the state allows it a set return.
cpt: Camden has one business: it builds, buys and rents out apartments in Sun Belt cities such as Charlotte and Nashville.
cvx: Chevron pumps oil and gas and refines it into fuel, but most of its profit comes from the pumping, not the refining.
dltr: Dollar Tree built its brand on one fixed price, $1 then $1.25, and has moved most of its stores to several price points.
ed: Con Edison is New York City's licensed power monopoly: it wins no customers and earns a set return on its grid.
ess: Essex only owns apartments in three West Coast metros — Southern California, the Bay Area and Seattle.
fds: FactSet rents the data screen investment pros stare at all day, sold by subscription, so almost all its revenue repeats.
frt: Federal Realty is the landlord you visit without noticing: open-air shopping centers and streets mixing shops and homes.
gm: GM sells over $180 billion of vehicles a year, but almost all its profit comes from big pickup trucks and SUVs.
hig: The Hartford is two insurers in one: business cover driven by weather and lawsuits, and employee benefits by jobs.
hum: Humana insures seniors on Medicare and owns the clinics that treat them — healthy patients mean bigger profit.
iqv: IQVIA runs clinical trials for drug companies and also sells them the prescription data they use to market drugs.
key: KeyCorp runs branches and its own investment bank, KeyBanc, so it can lend to mid-sized firms and advise them on deals.
lhx: L3Harris and one rival are effectively the only Western makers of solid rocket motors for missiles.
maa: MAA owns and rents out over 100,000 apartments in 16 states, mostly across the Southeast and Southwest.
mlm: Martin Marietta mines crushed stone that's too heavy to truck far, giving each quarry a local monopoly for miles around.
msi: Motorola Solutions sells police and fire radios, then earns years of software and service fees on the networks.
noc: Northrop builds the only new Western stealth bomber, on a fixed-price contract that has cost it billions in losses.
oke: ONEOK gathers, processes, ships and stores natural gas and its liquids, earning mostly fees, not betting on prices.
pfe: Pfizer sells medicines and vaccines, and four drugs that made up a third of its sales lose patent protection by 2030.
ppg: PPG began as Pittsburgh Plate Glass; now it makes only coatings, for drink cans, new cars, aircraft and body shops.
reg: Regency's supermarket tenants pay only a fifth of the rent, but the traffic they bring lets other tenants pay more.
ry: Royal Bank of Canada leads a banking market dominated by five big banks, which lets it earn unusually high returns.
snps: Synopsys sells the software used to design nearly every chip — a failed chip costs far more than the software could.
sw: Smurfit Westrock makes cardboard boxes — too bulky to ship far, so it wins by owning mills near customers.
tgt: Target's stores double as its warehouses — most online orders are picked and packed from the same shelves shoppers use.
tsm: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker: it builds chips others design and sells none under its own name.
unh: UnitedHealth insures you, employs your doctor and processes the claim — one company, start to finish.
vrt: Vertiv doesn't make AI chips — it makes the power and cooling systems every AI server rack has to sit inside.
wm: Waste Management's landfills can't be copied, so rival haulers without one nearby must pay WM to dump their trash.
zbh: Zimmer Biomet's customer isn't the patient — it's the surgeon, who rarely wants to relearn a new set of instruments.
aee: Ameren has a legal monopoly on the wires in its patch, but three separate regulators decide what return it may earn.
alny: Alnylam's drugs don't block a harmful protein; they destroy the cell's instructions for it, so the body never makes it.
aph: Amphenol sells connectors through over 100 near-independent units, each with its own boss and its own profit target.
azo: AutoZone sells car parts, but its suppliers fund the shelves: it owes vendors more than the stock it holds is worth.
bkng: Booking Holdings owns no hotels — it takes a commission on rooms, and increasingly holds the cash itself.
cah: Cardinal Health is one of three firms moving nearly all US drugs, and keeps under a penny per sales dollar as profit.
chd: Church & Dwight grows by buying small brands that lead a niche, like Zicam, TheraBreath and Hero, then scaling them up.
cnc: Centene insures Medicaid patients at a rate states fix a year ahead of knowing how sick they'll be.
crh: CRH's real asset is its quarries: rock is too costly to haul far, and new pits near growing cities rarely get permits.
d: Dominion is a regulated utility whose Virginia grid happens to sit under the world's largest cluster of data centers.
doc: Healthpeak rents healthcare buildings: doctors' offices beside hospitals, where 80% of tenants renew, plus biotech labs.
efx: Equifax is a credit bureau, but its best business is The Work Number: payroll data lenders pay to check what you earn.
etn: Eaton makes switchgear, the gear that routes a building's power. Engineers pick it years ahead; swapping it is costly.
fdx: FedEx runs a global air network so costly to build that express delivery is a three-player game: FedEx, UPS and DHL.
fslr: First Solar makes panels on glass without silicon, and a federal credit paid per US-made watt is most of its profit.
gnrc: Generac sells home standby generators through local installers, and big backup units to data centers that can't go dark.
hii: Huntington Ingalls is the only US shipyard that builds nuclear aircraft carriers, yet earns a single-digit margin.
hwm: Howmet casts jet-engine turbine blades, and once designed into an engine it sells the replacement blades for decades.
ir: Ingersoll Rand's compressors cost little next to the factory lines they keep running, so buyers rarely haggle on spares.
keys: Keysight builds test gear before the technology it tests even exists, giving engineers something to measure against.
lii: Lennox's air conditioners are chosen by the contractor standing in your basement, not by the homeowner paying for them.
mar: Marriott owns under 1% of its rooms. It mostly collects brand and management fees on hotels other people own.
mmm: 3M turns a handful of adhesive, film and abrasive technologies into roughly 60,000 different products.
mstr: Strategy still sells analytics software, but nearly all its value is bitcoin, bought with money raised by selling stock.
now: ServiceNow sells workflow software built on one map of every server and app a company runs, and that map is the lock-in.
omc: Omnicom owns ad agencies, but over half its core revenue is planning and buying media space for big brands.
pfg: Principal runs 401(k) plans — money keeps arriving by payroll even as savers move it to cheaper funds.
ppl: PPL is a regulated utility that earns a fixed rake on grid spending, set by three state regulators, not the market.
regn: Regeneron discovered Dupixent, yet Sanofi books all its sales. Regeneron records roughly half the profit instead.
sap: SAP's software holds a company's ledger, orders and payroll — replacing it is a multi-year project, not a purchase.
so: Southern runs monopoly grids in the Southeast and part-owns Vogtle 3 and 4, the only newly completed large US reactors.
swk: Stanley Black & Decker's lock-in is the battery: a contractor with a bag of DEWALT batteries buys the next DEWALT tool.
tjx: TJX doesn't order stock months ahead: it buys brands' cancelled orders and overruns at a discount, then sells them fast.
tsn: Tyson sells beef, chicken, pork and brands like Jimmy Dean; beef is a thin spread between two prices it doesn't set.
unp: Union Pacific's western rail network couldn't be rebuilt at any price, and many shippers on it have no second railroad.
vrtx: Vertex is the only company with an approved drug that treats the cause of cystic fibrosis, not just its symptoms.
wmb: Williams doesn't sell gas — it charges a toll on pipe that moves it, paid whether or not the customer ships a molecule.
zbra: Zebra makes the scanners and handhelds a warehouse standardizes on — swapping vendors means retraining the entire floor.
aem: Agnico Eagle mines gold, about 85% of it in Canada, and lives on the gap between the gold price and its cost per ounce.
amat: Applied Materials doesn't make chips; it makes the machines that deposit, etch and polish the layers on each one.
apo: Apollo is two businesses in one: a fee-earning money manager, and Athene, which earns the spread on annuity savings.
ba: Boeing is one of the two companies that build the world's big passenger jets, and also builds warplanes and satellites.
bkr: Baker Hughes gets filed as oilfield services, but half of it builds gas turbines for gas-export plants and data centers.
carr: Carrier makes gear that moves heat: air conditioners, heat pumps, chillers, and refrigeration for trucks and containers.
chrw: C.H. Robinson owns no trucks. It matches shippers with truckers and keeps the difference between what each side pays.
cni: CN is one of Canada's two big freight railroads, hauling goods by rail and truck across Canada and into the U.S.
crl: Before a drug reaches humans, someone proves it's safe in animals. Charles River breeds the rats and runs those tests.
dal: Delta sells seats, but American Express also pays it billions a year for SkyMiles points earned on Delta-branded cards.
dov: Dover makes the nozzle on the fuel pump, the printer that stamps use-by dates and the store fridge: a stack of niches.
eg: Everest mostly insures other insurance companies, taking on risk they'd rather not carry alone.
etr: Entergy is a regulated utility in four Southern states. It earns an approved return on what it builds, not on sales.
fdxf: FedEx Freight is North America's largest carrier of part-truckload shipments, about 90,000 a day through 365 terminals.
ftnt: Fortinet designs its own security chip rather than buying one, letting it sell cheaper firewalls at fatter margins.
googl: Alphabet is Google: about 55% of its revenue is search ads, from an engine handling about 9 in 10 of all web searches.
hlt: Hilton owns almost none of its hotels, about 1% of rooms, so nearly all its profit is fees on other people's buildings.
ibkr: Interactive Brokers is a stock brokerage, but more than half its revenue is interest on customer cash and margin loans.
irm: Iron Mountain still earns about 70% of its revenue storing boxes of paper, and uses that rent to build data centers.
khc: Kraft Heinz lives on old pantry brands: Heinz ketchup, Kraft mac and cheese, Oscar Mayer and Capri Sun.
lin: Linde sells industrial gases, half under 10- to 20-year contracts where customers pay whether or not they use the gas.
mas: Masco makes Delta faucets and Behr paint, sold mostly for home repairs and remodels rather than new-house building.
mnst: Monster owns the energy-drink brands; Coca-Cola's bottlers get the cans into stores, and Coca-Cola owns a stake.
mtb: M&T Bank's edge is cheap deposits: nearly 29% pay no interest, funding a loan book heavy in commercial real estate.
nrg: NRG makes electricity and sells it to about eight million customers, so its own plants partly hedge its retail arm.
on: onsemi makes power chips that switch high voltages in electric cars and AI data centers, many built on silicon carbide.
pg: P&G sells about 20 billion-dollar brands like Tide and Pampers, and spends $8B a year on ads to keep them premium.
pru: Prudential is a U.S. insurer, but its largest single profit pool is life insurance sold abroad, overwhelmingly in Japan.
rf: Regions is the default checking account of the American South, and those cheap deposits fund a plain-vanilla lender.
sbac: SBA owns over 46,000 cell-tower sites and rents space on them to phone carriers on long leases with yearly rent rises.
solv: Solventum is the old 3M health-care business: it sells wound-care and surgical supplies and dental products.
swks: Skyworks makes the radio chips that connect phones to networks; mobile is over half its sales, Apple its biggest buyer.
tko: TKO owns the UFC and WWE outright, so the fighters' contracts, the events and the TV rights all sit inside one company.
tt: Trane sells heating and cooling systems, but about a third of its revenue is servicing machines it already installed.
ups: UPS carries about a fifth of America's packages but earns roughly a third of the industry's parcel revenue.
vst: Vistra runs power plants and sells electricity to about 5 million retail customers, so its own plants act as the hedge.
wmt: Walmart is America's biggest grocer, but its fastest-growing profits are ads, membership fees and online marketplace.
zts: Zoetis makes medicines and vaccines for animals, and about 70% of its sales are for pets such as dogs, cats and horses.
adi: Analog Devices makes chips that turn real-world signals into data, and many stay in production for decades.
alb: Albemarle produces lithium for batteries but can't set its price, so its profit can swing four-fold on that one input.
aon: Aon doesn't insure anything itself; it earns fees connecting companies to insurers, keeping none of the risk.
avy: Avery Dennison makes the blank label stock and RFID tags that other companies print and stick onto their goods.
bfb: Brown-Forman sells Jack Daniel's distilled years ago, so its money sits in aging whiskey that no rival can simply buy.
bsx: Boston Scientific makes medical devices, and about two-thirds of its sales come from heart and blood-vessel care.
cdw: CDW doesn't make any of the technology it sells; it configures, finances and ships other firms' hardware.
cme: CME doesn't need markets to rise or fall, only to move; traders who clear with it save $95 billion a day in collateral.
cp: Canadian Pacific Kansas City is the only railway with an unbroken line connecting Canada, the US and Mexico.
ctva: Corteva sells crop chemicals and Pioneer seeds, and the seed genetics it also licenses out earn nearly twice the margin.
dhr: Danaher's filters and resins for making drugs are written into a drug's approval filing, so switching means re-testing.
ebay: eBay holds no stock; it takes a fee on each sale, and about a fifth of its revenue is ads sold to its own sellers.
eqt: EQT is the largest US natural gas producer, yet its gas sells below the national price for lack of pipeline out.
fang: Diamondback pumps Permian crude, and the natural gas that comes up with it is sometimes worth less than nothing.
flex: Flex builds electronics for other brands, from car systems to medical gear, keeping about three cents per sales dollar.
gis: General Mills owns Blue Buffalo pet food, but cereal and baking staples like Cheerios earn about two-thirds of profit.
hca: HCA runs America's largest for-profit hospital chain, and by law its emergency rooms must treat patients who can't pay.
hst: Host Hotels owns about 75 luxury hotels but employs fewer than 200 people; Marriott and other brands run them for a fee.
intu: Intuit is best known for TurboTax, but about 60% of its revenue comes from QuickBooks and other small-business software.
jkhy: Jack Henry runs the nightly ledgers of over 7,000 small banks and credit unions, and switching that system takes years.
ldos: Leidos builds intelligence software and missile-warning satellites, and runs the medical exams behind veterans' claims.
lyb: LyondellBasell makes the raw plastic most packaging starts as, and is the largest licensor of the know-how to make it.
meta: Meta earns about 98% of its money from ads on Facebook, Instagram and its other apps, while pouring billions into AI.
ms: Morgan Stanley is mostly two equal halves: Wall Street banking and trading, and wealth advice that earns steady fees.
nflx: Netflix earns mostly from subscriptions in about 190 countries, and over a third of what members watch isn't in English.
nwsa: News Corp owns the Wall Street Journal, but its top-earning business is property-listings websites, not newspapers.
pdd: PDD owns Pinduoduo and Temu, earning ad and sales fees from merchants, and it never discloses Temu's own numbers.
pnr: Pentair makes gear that moves and cleans water, from farm pumps and home softeners to backyard pool equipment.
race: Ferrari could sell more cars than it builds, but it deliberately ships fewer, letting the waiting list keep prices up.
rsg: Republic Services collects trash, but most of it lands in landfills it owns, which are nearly impossible to permit.
smci: Supermicro builds the servers AI runs on, packed with Nvidia chips, but assembling them earns only thin margins.
stt: State Street safekeeps over $50 trillion of investments it doesn't own, earning a tiny fee on their value.
tel: TE Connectivity's connectors cost a few dollars, but requalifying a rival's costs far more than it saves.
trow: T. Rowe Price earns a fee on the money it manages, and stock funds pay the most, so a shift to bonds cuts its revenue.
uhs: Universal Health Services runs hospitals and psychiatric wards, and the psychiatric side earns most of the profit.
vmrk: Vivmark Residential builds, buys and rents out over 184,000 apartments, mostly in expensive coastal US cities.
wec: WEC Energy is a legal monopoly: in its territory, no rival utility is allowed to string a second set of wires.
xyl: Xylem makes water pumps, meters and treatment gear, and also runs clients' water systems on decades-long contracts.
